summary: Specifies a framework for adding a Carrier-Grade NAT layer to an operator's network using BGP/MPLS IP VPNs for routing separation. It addresses IPv4 address exhaustion and does not try to defend CGN itself.

plainLanguage.summary: Running low on addresses, a provider shares one address among many homes. This describes a way to add that sharing box by using separate private lanes.

questions: carrier grade nat with mpls vpn
subtitle: Using MPLS VPNs to integrate carrier-grade NAT in operator networks

tldr.problem: IPv4 addresses are running out, forcing operators to deploy Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) to share one public address among many homes. However, integrating CGN into existing networks creates routing and architecture challenges without disrupting traditional IPv4 services.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7289 describes a framework using BGP/MPLS IP VPNs to segregate CGN translation flows into separate virtual routing instances, allowing traffic to be routed independently to translators while keeping traditional IPv4 flows on their existing paths.
tldr.outcome: Operators can deploy CGN at centralized or distributed locations, bypass translation for local services, support overlapping private addresses, and provide IPv4 connectivity during the transition to IPv6.

facts.label: Primary technique
facts.value: BGP/MPLS IP VPNs with VRF separation

facts.label: Address space support
facts.value: IPv4 overlap within zones, Shared Address Space (RFC 6598)

today: RFC 7289 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It continues to be used by internet service providers deploying Carrier-Grade NAT to manage IPv4 address exhaustion while transitioning toward full IPv6 deployment. The BGP/MPLS VPN framework has been validated in production environments and remains a practical integration model for CGN infrastructure.

sections.title: CGN and IPv4 Exhaustion
sections.content:
Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN), also called Large-Scale NAT, is a Network Address Translation layer that an operator deploys in its network to allow many subscribers to share a small pool of public IPv4 addresses. This is a response to IPv4 address exhaustion: as the global supply of unused IPv4 addresses runs out, operators cannot assign globally unique addresses to all customers. Although IPv6 is the strategic answer, the near-term need for IPv4 connectivity may not be satisfied by IPv6 alone.

This RFC does not argue for or against CGN; instead, it provides a practical framework for integrating CGN into operator networks that already have active IPv4 and IPv6 services. The challenge is to add the translation layer in a way that minimizes disruption to existing services while meeting the technical challenges that CGN introduces.
sections.plainLanguage: There aren't enough internet addresses for everyone. Operators must put a 'translation box' that maps many homes to a few addresses. This RFC explains how to add that box without breaking the network.

sections.title: CGN Network Requirements
sections.content: Deploying CGN raises several architectural requirements. First, the deployment must support both centralized (few, large translation points) and distributed models (many, smaller ones). Early deployment might be centralized due to low demand, but over time as CGN usage grows, operators may need to distribute translators. Second, CGN-mediated flows (requiring translation) must coexist with traditional IPv4 flows (using public addresses), since both types of customers will exist for years. Third, CGN infrastructure should provide bypass for flows that don't need translation, such as internal DNS, email, and web caching services within the provider's network. Fourth, the routing plane must be separated between CGN flows and traditional IPv4 flows, since they have different routing needs and may use overlapping private address space. Fifth, the design should be flexible enough to move, split, or reconfigure translation points over time. Sixth, it must support common access technologies (DSL, cable, mobile, Ethernet). Seventh, the design must allow IPv4 address overlap (reusing the same private addresses in different translation zones). Finally, the system requires transactional logging of translation mappings for legal compliance and abuse mitigation.
sections.plainLanguage: CGN deployment must handle centralized or distributed translators, coexist with normal addresses, skip translation for internal services, separate routing paths, change over time, work with all network types, allow address reuse in zones, and log what gets translated.

sections.title: BGP/MPLS IP VPN Framework
sections.content:
The RFC proposes using BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, defined in RFC 4364, to solve these requirements. Each translation realm (a group of subscribers sharing a translation zone) is segregated into a separate MPLS-based VPN with its own routing instance called a Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF). Each VPN has a unique Route Distinguisher (RD) and Route Target (RT) combination, allowing independent routing control.

In this model, an access node (such as a DOCSIS CMTS or DSL BRAS) receives traffic from Customer Premises Equipment (CPE). If a subscriber has a public IPv4 address, traffic goes to the Global Routing Table (GRT) for direct internet routing. If a subscriber has a private address requiring translation, traffic goes to the CGN VRF, which uses an MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) to forward the traffic to a VRF termination point (a provider edge router where the CGN translator may reside). The translator then converts the private source address to a public address and forwards the translated traffic to the GRT for internet delivery. Once translated, the return path follows the standard internet routing back to the translator, which reverses the translation before the traffic returns to the subscriber through the access node.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS VPNs create separate virtual lanes. One lane carries private addresses to a translator. Another lane carries public addresses directly to the internet. A third lane can deliver internal services without translation. The access point picks which lane for each customer.

sections.title: Deployment Advantages
sections.content:
The BGP/MPLS IP VPN framework offers several advantages. Service separation is natural: the access node can route CGN customers to one VPN and traditional IPv4 customers to another, without complex policy-based routing. Internal service delivery can use a separate Services VRF where flows destined for operator-provided services (DNS, NTP, email) bypass the translator, reducing translator load and providing better paths. Dual-stack operation is supported: IPv4 flows can use the CGN VRF while IPv6 flows go directly to the GRT or an IPv6-specific VPN. Deployment flexibility is high because the physical location of the VRF termination point (where the translator resides) can be changed dynamically; if an operator needs to add more capacity or move a translator, the MPLS LSP paths adjust automatically without reconfiguring access nodes or routing policies.

The RFC also notes that IPv4 address overlap between zones is possible with route filtering and the VRF model, and redundancy can be implemented with backup default routes or other failover mechanisms without requiring a single prescribed redundancy model.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework is flexible: you can move translators, add new zones, bypass translation for internal services, and run IPv4 and IPv6 together. No complex routing policies needed.

sections.title: Comparison with Alternative Approaches
sections.content: The RFC briefly compares the BGP/MPLS VPN option with other possible integration methods. Policy-based routing (PBR) can direct CGN traffic to translators but requires static configuration throughout the network with high maintenance overhead and doesn't achieve service separation easily. Traffic engineering (MPLS with Traffic Engineering extensions) can achieve similar goals but adds complexity in setup and maintenance, and TE paths must be updated each time translation points change. Multiple routing topologies (running multiple routing protocol instances) could achieve the goals but with even higher implementation overhead and platform configuration complexity. By comparison, the BGP/MPLS VPN approach uses existing VPN infrastructure that many operators already have deployed, making it more practical for adoption.
sections.plainLanguage: Policy-based routing is simpler but hard to change. Traffic engineering is powerful but complex. MPLS VPNs are a middle ground that operators already know.

sections.title: Operational Experience
sections.content: The RFC notes that the MPLS/VPN CGN environment has been successfully integrated into real network environments and tested in production-network models. The framework solves key integration issues including support for centralized and distributed deployment, routing plane separation, flexible translation point design with low maintenance overhead, CGN bypass for internal services, IPv4 address overlap support between zones, and simple failover techniques. The model has been validated with existing IPv4 and IPv6 services and continues to be used by operators managing IPv4 address exhaustion while transitioning toward IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators have tested this model in real networks and it works. It manages IPv4 exhaustion while they move toward IPv6.
